title: One city
hookLine: if reason is shared and law is shared, we're fellow citizens of one city (Meditations 4.4)

cards: Somebody once asked the philosopher Diogenes where he came from. The usual answer would have been a town: Sinope, on the Black Sea. Instead, the old story says, he answered: I am a citizen of the world.

The Greek word was kosmopolites, where we get cosmopolitan. Five hundred years later, an emperor who ruled much of the known world built an argument under that one-liner, step by careful step. Today: one city.

teach.b: Marcus begins the fourth entry of book four: if the power to think is common to all of us, then reason, which makes us reasoning creatures, is common too. You and the stranger at the bus stop have the same equipment.
If reason is common, he goes on, then the reason that tells us what to do and not do is common. And if that's common, law is common. And if law is common, we are fellow citizens.
We share in a kind of political life, and so the world is, in a way, a city.

What other shared constitution, he asks, could the whole human race be said to share? He ends by asking where else our minds, our reason and our sense of law could come from, if not from this common source.
Just as the earth, water, air and fire in his body come from somewhere, so does his mind. Notice what this does to a stranger.
If you and the person cutting in line are citizens of one city, they're not an obstacle or an extra in your movie.

teach.h: WHERE ELSE WOULD MIND COME FROM?
teach.b: They're a neighbor, maybe a badly behaved one, but a neighbor. Seneca, a few weeks back on this path, spoke of two cities, the local one and the great one.
Marcus folds them closer: one city, and you were born in it. Elsewhere he says it plainly. A poet calls Athens dear city of Cecrops.
Won't you call the world dear city of Zeus?

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often recall Meditations 4.4 with strangers, reminding themselves that shared reason makes everyone a fellow citizen of one world-city.

o: a single planned city where everyone lives alike
one capital city ruling over every nation on earth
the whole world as one city, since all people share reason

s: Marcus invented the idea of being a citizen of the world
the old story gives that answer to Diogenes, centuries earlier.
Marcus argues step by step from shared reason to one city
reason, then law, then citizenship, then the world as a city.
'cosmopolitan' comes from a Greek word for world-citizen
kosmopolites: kosmos, world, and polites, citizen.

games.q: a stranger at the airport is rude to the gate agent, then sits next to you. what fits Meditations 4.4?
o: treat them as an obstacle and ignore them.
treat them as a neighbor, a badly behaved one.
tell them what you think of them.
games.why: if reason and law are shared, Marcus says, we're fellow citizens: even the rude stranger lives in your city.

practice: Picture a stranger you'll probably pass today, a cashier, a driver, someone on the sidewalk, as clearly as you can. Say to yourself, gently: same reason, same law, same city. Notice whether anything shifts in you.

wordCard.voice: One city. Marcus reasons that shared reason means shared law, and shared law means we are all fellow citizens of one world-city. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'city, city-state': Marcus says the whole world is, in a way, one polis.

carryVoice: Your line: dear city of Zeus. The stranger in line is a neighbor too. That's day five hundred fifty-two.
